notes.b: Some genes sit on the sex chromosomes rather than on the other chromosomes, and this changes how they are inherited. Because males and females carry different sex chromosomes, the same allele can have a different effect in each sex.
points: Sex-linked genes are almost all on the X chromosome (X-linked), because the Y carries very few genes.
A sex-linked trait is a trait controlled by such a gene. The Y has no matching allele for most X-linked genes, so in males the X-linked gene has no second copy to pair with.
Females (XX) have two copies of each X-linked gene, so they can be homozygous (two identical alleles) or heterozygous (two different alleles).
A heterozygous female with one recessive allele is a carrier (she carries the allele but does not show the trait), because her dominant allele masks it.
Males (XY) have only one copy, so whatever allele their single X carries is expressed, with no second allele to mask it.
This is why a male cannot be a carrier, and why one recessive allele is enough for him to show the trait.
X-linked recessive conditions are therefore much more common in males than in females.
A female shows the condition only if she inherits the recessive allele from both parents, which means an affected father and a carrier or affected mother.
notes.tip: If asked why sex-linked recessive conditions are more common in males, say that males have only one X, so a single recessive allele is expressed. Remember that sex-linked does not mean the trait affects only one sex.

notes.h: How a father and a mother pass on X-linked alleles (Higher Level only)
notes.b: To predict who inherits an X-linked allele, follow the sex chromosomes. A child's sex is decided by the sex chromosome the father contributes, and that also decides where the X-linked allele comes from.
points: A father passes his X to all his daughters and his Y to all his sons.
So an affected father never passes an X-linked condition to his sons, because sons get his Y, which carries no allele for the gene.
All his daughters are at least carriers, because each receives his X with the recessive allele.
A son's X-linked allele always comes from his mother, since his only X is the one she gave him.
notes.tip: Examiners ask about the children of a carrier mother and a normal or affected father. Work out which parent each child's X comes from before writing any genotype.

notes.h: Symbols for X-linked alleles (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Genetics questions use a fixed way of writing X-linked genotypes so that the sex and the alleles are both clear at a glance.
points: Write the allele as a superscript on the X, and the Y with no allele, because the Y has no matching allele for these genes.
Colour blindness: Xᴮ = normal colour vision, Xᵇ = colour blind. Haemophilia: Xᴴ = normal clotting, Xʰ = haemophilia.
Colour-blindness genotypes: female XᴮXᴮ (normal), XᴮXᵇ (carrier), XᵇXᵇ (colour blind); male XᴮY (normal), XᵇY (colour blind).
Use the letters a question gives.
notes.tip: Write the Y with no allele (XᵇY, not XᵇYᵇ), and never call a male a carrier of an X-linked trait.

notes.b: Red-green colour blindness is the standard example of an X-linked recessive condition, and the one most often used in crosses.
points: Red-green colour blindness is an X-linked recessive condition in which a person has difficulty telling red and green apart.

The genes for the red- and green-sensitive light-absorbing pigments of the cone cells of the retina (the colour-detecting cells at the back of the eye) are on the X chromosome. The recessive allele gives a pigment that is missing or works abnormally.
It affects about 1 in 12 men (8%) and about 1 in 200 women (0.5%) of northern European ancestry. The difference fits the pattern that males need only one recessive allele.
It is detected with coloured-dot test charts (Ishihara plates).
It is not treatable, but most people adapt to it.
notes.tip: Be ready to name a sex-linked condition and give one fact about it, such as that it is X-linked recessive and detected with Ishihara plates.

notes.b: Haemophilia is the second named X-linked recessive condition. It shows how a single faulty gene can affect the whole body, because it removes one step in blood clotting.
points: Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive condition in which blood does not clot properly because a clotting protein is missing or faulty.
Haemophilia A lacks clotting factor VIII; haemophilia B lacks factor IX.
Bleeding after injury lasts much longer, and bleeding can occur into joints and muscles.
Haemophilia A affects about 1 in 5,000 male births.
It is treated by injections of the missing clotting factor, now mostly produced by genetically engineered cells. There is more on this in Genetic engineering.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to name a sex-linked condition, and sometimes one other than haemophilia, so know a second one as well.

notes.h: A historical example: Queen Victoria (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Haemophilia in European royal families is a well-known real case of an X-linked allele passing through carrier daughters to affected grandsons.
points: Queen Victoria (1819–1901) was a carrier of haemophilia.
Her son Leopold had haemophilia. Through two of her daughters, who were carriers, it passed into the royal families of Russia (Tsarevich Alexei, son of Tsar Nicholas II) and Spain.

notes.b: Haemophilia and colour blindness are not the only X-linked recessive conditions. A third example is useful when a question asks for one other than haemophilia.
points: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is another X-linked recessive condition, caused by a lack of the muscle protein dystrophin, which causes progressive muscle weakness (muscles get steadily weaker over time).
It is almost always in boys, which fits the pattern for X-linked recessive conditions.
notes.tip: Use Duchenne muscular dystrophy if a question asks for a sex-linked condition other than haemophilia.

notes.h: Carrier female × normal male (Higher Level only)
notes.b: This is the most common X-linked cross. A mother who is a carrier of colour blindness has a partner with normal vision, so we can work out what their children could inherit.
points: Parents' phenotypes: normal-vision (carrier) female × normal-vision male.
Parents' genotypes: carrier female XᴮXᵇ × normal male XᴮY.
Gametes (each carries one sex chromosome with its allele): carrier female Xᴮ, Xᵇ × normal male Xᴮ, Y.
Punnett square: XᴮXᴮ, XᴮY / XᴮXᵇ, XᵇY.
Offspring genotypes and phenotypes: 1 normal female (XᴮXᴮ) : 1 carrier female (XᴮXᵇ) : 1 normal male (XᴮY) : 1 colour-blind male (XᵇY).
Half the sons are expected to be colour blind and half the daughters carriers; no daughters are colour blind, because every daughter gets the father's normal Xᴮ. 25% of all children are colour blind.

Diagram: the Punnett square for this cross, with the mother's gametes Xᴮ and Xᵇ on one side and the father's Xᴮ and Y on the other, each box labelled with genotype and phenotype (normal female, carrier female, normal male, colour-blind male).
notes.tip: Give ratios for the right group: half the sons is not half the children. State whether a percentage is of sons, daughters or all children.

notes.h: Normal female × affected male (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Here the father has haemophilia and the mother has two normal alleles. This cross shows what an affected father passes on.
points: Parents' phenotypes: normal female × affected male.
Parents' genotypes: normal female XᴴXᴴ × affected male XʰY.
Gametes: normal female Xᴴ × affected male Xʰ, Y.
Offspring: XᴴXʰ (carrier daughters) and XᴴY (normal sons), 1 : 1.
All daughters are carriers, because each gets the father's Xʰ. No children have haemophilia, because the sons get his Y and the mother's normal Xᴴ.

notes.h: Carrier female × colour-blind male (Higher Level only)
notes.b: When both parents contribute a recessive allele, a daughter can be affected. This cross shows how that happens.
points: Parents' phenotypes: carrier female × colour-blind male.
Parents' genotypes: carrier female XᴮXᵇ × colour-blind male XᵇY.
Gametes: carrier female Xᴮ, Xᵇ × colour-blind male Xᵇ, Y.
Offspring: XᴮXᵇ (carrier female), XᵇXᵇ (colour-blind female), XᴮY (normal male), XᵇY (colour-blind male), 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.
Half the daughters and half the sons are colour blind. This is how a colour-blind daughter can arise: she inherits Xᵇ from both her mother and her father.

notes.h: Affected female × normal male (Higher Level only)
notes.b: This cross reverses the sexes of the affected parent. It shows that an affected mother passes the condition to every son.
points: Parents' phenotypes: affected female × normal male.
Parents' genotypes: affected female XʰXʰ × normal male XᴴY.
Gametes: affected female Xʰ × normal male Xᴴ, Y.
Offspring: XᴴXʰ (carrier daughters) and XʰY (sons with haemophilia).
All sons are affected, because their only X comes from the mother; all daughters are carriers, because they also get the father's normal Xᴴ.
Females with haemophilia are very rare; this cross is used to show the pattern.

notes.b: A pedigree shows how a trait passes through several generations of a family. Before you can use one, you need to know what its symbols and lines mean.
points: A pedigree is a family-tree diagram showing which members of a family have a trait.
Symbols: square = male; circle = female; shaded = affected; half-shaded (or a dot in the centre) = carrier.
A horizontal line joining a male and a female = parents; a vertical line down to a horizontal line = their children, in birth order from left to right.
Generations are numbered I, II, III and individuals 1, 2, 3 within each, so every person can be named, for example II-2.

notes.h: Signs of an X-linked recessive trait in a pedigree (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Four features of a pedigree point to an X-linked recessive trait. Each follows from the rules on how X chromosomes are passed on.
points: Many more affected males than females, because a male needs only one recessive allele.
Affected males usually have unaffected parents, because the mother is a carrier.
The trait can skip a generation, passing from an affected man through his carrier daughters to his grandsons.
It is never passed from father to son, because a son gets his father's Y, not his X.
notes.tip: In pedigree questions, use these signs to justify your answer, for example that no father passed the trait to a son.

notes.h: Solving a pedigree step by step (Higher Level only)
notes.b: To give the genotype of a named person, or the chance that a child is affected or a carrier, work through the pedigree in a fixed order. This starts with the people whose genotype is certain.
points: 1. Write XY for every male and XX for every female.
2. Fill in the alleles of affected males (XʰY) and unaffected males (XᴴY), which follow directly from their phenotype.
3. Any daughter of an affected male is at least a carrier; any mother of an affected son is a carrier or affected.
4. Use these to fill in the remaining females.
5. Then work any further cross with a Punnett square.

Diagram: a three-generation X-linked recessive pedigree. Generation I: normal man, carrier woman. Generation II: affected son, normal son, carrier daughter, normal daughter. Generation III: the carrier daughter's children with a normal man, including an affected grandson. Label symbols and generations.
notes.tip: Questions give a pedigree of haemophilia or colour blindness and ask for the genotypes of named individuals and the chance of a child of a given couple being affected or a carrier.

notes.b: Genes on the Y chromosome follow a different pattern from X-linked genes, because only males have a Y.
points: Genes on the Y chromosome (for example SRY) are passed only from father to son and are found only in males. There is more on SRY in Sex determination.
notes.tip: Sex-linkage is not sex determination, so do not mix them up.

keyTerms.definition: A trait controlled by a gene on a sex chromosome, most often the X chromosome.
A family-tree diagram showing which members of a family have a trait.
Coloured-dot test charts used to detect red-green colour blindness.
The muscle protein whose lack causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

questions.prompt: Explain why red-green colour blindness is more common in males than in females.
questions.model: The gene for red-green colour blindness is on the X chromosome, and the Y has no matching allele. Males have one X, so a single recessive allele on it is expressed. Females have two X chromosomes, so a female needs the recessive allele on both X chromosomes to show the condition; one copy makes her a carrier. Males are therefore affected far more often than females.

questions.prompt: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia has children with a man with normal blood clotting. Using a genetic cross, give the genotypes and phenotypes of the possible children, and the probability that a son will have haemophilia.
questions.model: Parents' phenotypes: carrier female × normal male. Parents' genotypes: XᴴXʰ × XᴴY. Gametes: Xᴴ, Xʰ × Xᴴ, Y. Punnett square: XᴴXᴴ, XᴴY / XᴴXʰ, XʰY. Offspring: XᴴXᴴ (normal daughter), XᴴXʰ (carrier daughter), XᴴY (normal son), XʰY (son with haemophilia), in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio. Probability: 50% of sons will have haemophilia, and 25% of all children will have haemophilia.

questions.prompt: A colour-blind man and a woman with normal vision whose father was colour blind have a daughter. Give the parents' genotypes and the probability that the daughter is colour blind.
questions.model: The woman's father was colour blind (XᵇY), so she received Xᵇ from him; she has normal vision, so she is XᴮXᵇ. The man is colour blind, so he is XᵇY. Cross: XᴮXᵇ × XᵇY, with gametes Xᴮ, Xᵇ × Xᵇ, Y. Offspring: XᴮXᵇ (carrier daughter), XᵇXᵇ (colour-blind daughter), XᴮY (normal son), XᵇY (colour-blind son). Half of the daughters are XᵇXᵇ, so the probability that the daughter is colour blind is 1/2.
